newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: FEATURE - Asia in ambitious plan to take lead out of petrol.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Asia in ambitious plan to take lead out of petrol.

text.p: It took the United States 23 years to phase out lead in petrol, but Thailand managed the feat in five years and now China aims to get it done in less than four.

Increasingly, countries in the Asia-Pacific region are embarking on aggressive programmes to get rid of lead in petrol as new evidence reveals the harmful effects of the pollutant on people and the environment.

"Lead impairs the mental development of children and causes cardiovascular diseases in adults even at low levels of exposure which were previously considered safe," Magda Lovei, an environmental economist at the World Bank, told a conference on cleaner burning motor fuels this month.
"A loss of three to six IQ points in urban children has been attributed to exposures to lead in Bangkok, Cairo, Manila and Jakarta," she said.
Such worrying statistics have intensified the fight against these pollutants but efforts to come up with a successful plan are often thwarted by either high costs or a lack of political will.
The Asia-Pacific consumes about 2.8 million barrels of petrol a day. About 37 percent of this contains lead. Another 12 percent has a high content of harmful chemicals.
ECONOMIC STATUS NOT AN EXCUSE
Of the 20 countries worldwide which have phased out lead in petrol, only two are from the Asia-Pacific region -- Japan and Thailand.
"It indicated economic development is not the only factor that affects this process," Lovei said.
Most Asian countries have a maximum lead content of 0.15 grammes per litre, but a small number such as Indonesia and Vietnam allow larger lead contents of up to 0.45 grammes.

The World Bank, which helped Thailand in its programme to phase out lead, said policy measures such as the deregulation of oil prices and the removal of restrictions on the private sector were necessary for success.
"Government commitment is necessary to tackle the problem and regulate the use of lead and the content of other harmful substance in gasoline," Lovei said.
Thailand's success story is clearly seen by the sharp decline of lead in its air.
In 1996, the monthly average lead level in Bangkok fell to 0.10 microgrammes per cubic metre, compared with 2.0 microgrammes in 1990.
The new level is well below the world standard of 1.5 microgrammes, Oranut Paisarnuchapong of the Thai Pollution Control Department told the Singapore conference.
Oranut said Thailand's success was down to the government's concerted effort to beat the problem through a national plan that covered all sectors.

"Those measures focused not only at emission standards for vehicles, but also at the improvement of fuel quality and engine specification, better traffic management and improvement of public transportation through mass transit systems," he said.
CHINA TAKING TOUGH APPROACH TO ELIMINATE LEAD
China is also taking a similarly tough approach to eliminate lead from its petrol by the end of 2000, said Li Pei, a senior official at the Chinese National Environmental Protection Agency.
Li told Reuters after addressing the conference that the Chinese government would announce an action plan in November for phasing out leaded petrol.

The plan would outline steps to be taken for the production of new vehicles that can use unleaded petrol and modifications to old ones, as well as fiscal incentives to encourage the use of unleaded petrol.
"Our automotive industry is changing the production of cars to use unleaded petrol and have catalytic converters," Li said.

She said Chinese laws on air pollution were amended in 1995 to say that "relevant competent departments shall devise plans for gradual decrease of lead petrol production, until its production and usage discontinue".
ASIA LOOKS TO LEARN FROM UNITED STATES
The Asia-Pacific region is looking to the United States, the world's largest petrol consumer, for direction on the formulation of the petrol of the future.
The U.S.-mandated reformulated petrol programme requires a 2.0 percent oxygen content by weight and a maximum benzene content of 1.0 percent in conventional petrol.

Blakeman Early, environmental consultant at the American Lung Association, said a limit on the use of benzene had been made because refiners used the chemical in petrol to replace the octane lost with the removal of lead.

"This created gasoline that was more volatile, contributing to smog creation. The addition of benzene, a known human cancer-causing chemical, and other suspected carcinogens, has increased ambient levels of these chemicals," Early said.
As a result of the U.S. experience, the Asia-Pacific region is keeping a close watch on how much of these chemicals are put into petrol as lead is phased out.
Many countries are also limiting benzene and aromatic content to less than two and 25 percent from about five and 50 percent at present, analysts said.
The rewards for such tough actions are plentiful.

A U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) study on the use of cleaner fuel between 1970 and 1990 found that for every $1 invested in reducing air pollution, around $45 was returned in benefits to the U.S. economy from reduced health care costs, other health effects and crop damage.
